title: The attack on Nat Cole on stage in Birmingham
summary: Men rushed the stage and one hit Nat before detectives pulled him off; the next morning over 100 white people apologized at the airport.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh, they came up on stage to get him. The women really saved him, though, really, because they saw them going toward the stage and the women started screaming, and they had detectives all over the place, and the guy -- he did get up and hit Nat, but a detective grabbed him and was pulling him off him and the detectives ran from offstage, and so I'm telling Ted for the band to play The Star Spangled Banner, and so they started playing Save the Queen, you know. Save the Queen ... save somebody. So Spark is over there

saying, 'Get on off the stage!' It was really quite a thing. And you got to be used to that type of thing, because after it happened, I was really disgusted, you know, and so I lived about 8 blocks from the motel, and I wasn't used to that; I didn't know. And I started walking, and I walked to the motel, and when I got to the motel, everybody was scared to death; they thought that something had happened to me because they said, 'It's a wonder that they had not picked you up off the street' because during that time, they were doing those kinds of things.
The Sparky you mentioned was Sparky Tavares?
Yeah, Sparky Tavares, you know, he was with us for years. He's now with Nancy Wilson.
Oh, as the band boy, road manager?
Yeah, he's the whole thing -- he's the whole shot.
How many people came up on the stage?
Didn't but one get there, but 5 of them were coming. They were intercepted, though.
Did they have any weapons or anything?

No, they were just coming to beat him, I guess, and kick him and stomp him, whatever they do down there. But you know, there again, we were at the airport the next morning -- it's really ironic the way things happen --

now you're fogged in and you really want to get out of Birmingham. No you're fogged in, and do you know, while we were fogged in, I would venture to guess over 100 people came to the airport apologizing, you know, saying how ashamed they were that this happened in their city, you know.

Yes, all white people. You could not -- that was why I say that you cannot blame -- you just can't speak in total, you can't just say everybody is rotten, you know, because they didn't have to do that, but they felt embarrassed and they just didn't want to be a part of that, and I thought that was commendable, you know, but then we had to cancel quite a bit of the tour, in the South, anyway.
